passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a high‑protein diet on the growth of laboratory rats over a 5‑week period. Forty male Sprague‑Dawley rats were randomly assigned to either a control diet (10% protein) or a high‑protein diet (30% protein). Body weights were recorded weekly. Table 1 gives the mean weights and standard deviations of the high‑protein group at each week; control‑group values are not shown. The authors reported that the high‑protein group gained weight more rapidly than the control group. The authors concluded that increased protein intake accelerates growth in adolescent rats and recommended further investigation into the underlying metabolic mechanisms.
stem: Which week had the highest mean weight in the high‑protein group?
explanation: The table shows a progressive increase in mean weight each week, reaching the maximum of 260 g in week 5.
trap: Students often assume the peak occurs earlier because the growth curve appears steep at week 3, but the data confirm week 5 is highest.

stem: Which experimental control would best isolate the effect of protein on weight gain?

options.A: Use a group of rats fed a high‑fat diet.
options.B: Use a group of rats fed the same caloric intake but with 10% protein.
options.C: Use a group of rats with no diet intervention.
options.D: Use a group of rats fed a low‑carbohydrate diet.

explanation: Keeping caloric intake constant while varying only protein content isolates protein as the variable affecting weight gain.
trap: Students may think a high‑fat or low‑carbohydrate group is a control, but those introduce other macronutrient variables.

stem: What is the percent change in mean weight from week 1 to week 5?
trap: Dividing the 60 g gain by the week-5 weight (260 g) gives about 23%; percent change must use the week-1 weight (200 g) as the denominator.

stem: Which statement is NOT supported by Table 1?

options.A: The weekly weight gain in week 5 (20 g) was larger than in week 2 (10 g).
options.B: The high‑protein diet produced a greater mean weight than the control at all time points.
options.C: Standard deviation increased over the study period.
options.D: The high‑protein group's mean weight rose every week.

explanation: Correct: B) Table 1 lists only the high-protein group, so a comparison with control means at each time point cannot be made. Why the others are wrong: A) Gains were 10 g (week 1 to 2) and 20 g (week 4 to 5). C) SD rose from 5 to 9 g. D) Means rose 200, 210, 225, 240, 260 g.
trap: Assuming the control group followed the same pattern, when Table 1 presents values only for the high-protein group.

stem: Which conclusion is best supported by Table 1?

options.A: The high‑protein group's mean weight rose from 200 g to 260 g over the five weeks.
options.B: The high‑protein diet increased muscle mass.
options.C: Caloric intake was the primary driver of weight gain.
options.D: The table proves that protein causes growth in all rats.

explanation: Correct: A) The table gives 200 g at week 1 and 260 g at week 5. Why the others are wrong: B) Only body weight was measured, not muscle mass. C) Caloric intake was not reported. D) A table of one group's means cannot prove causation or generalize to all rats.
trap: Reading a rise in body weight as evidence of muscle growth or proven causation, when only weights were measured.
